title: MATH GAOKAO - 299
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Find the area under a parabola over a closed interval using a definite integral.
questions.question: Find the area under the curve \(y=x^2\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=1\).
questions.explanation:
The area is given by the definite integral
\[
\int_{0}^{1}x^2\,dx.
\]
An antiderivative of \(x^2\) is \(\frac{x^3}{3}\). Thus,
\[
\int_{0}^{1}x^2\,dx
=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}
=\frac{1}{3}-0
=\frac{1}{3}.
\]
questions.hint: Set up the definite integral with limits \(0\) and \(1\), then use the power rule for antiderivatives.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the area under a linear curve over an interval using a definite integral.
questions.question: Find the area under the curve \(y=2x\) from \(x=1\) to \(x=3\).
questions.explanation:
The area is
\[
\int_{1}^{3}2x\,dx.
\]
An antiderivative of \(2x\) is \(x^2\). Therefore,
\[
\int_{1}^{3}2x\,dx
=\left[x^2\right]_{1}^{3}
=3^2-1^2
=9-1
=8.
\]
questions.hint: Evaluate the definite integral of \(2x\) from \(1\) to \(3\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the area under \(y=\sin x\) over one nonnegative half-period.
questions.question: Find the area under the curve \(y=\sin x\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=\pi\).
questions.explanation:
The area is
\[
\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx.
\]
An antiderivative of \(\sin x\) is \(-\cos x\). Thus,
\[
\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx
=\left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi}
=-\cos\pi-(-\cos0)
=-(-1)+1
=2.
\]
questions.hint: The function \(\sin x\) is nonnegative on \([0,\pi]\), so the area equals the definite integral.

questions.learningObjective: Find the area under \(y=e^x\) over a logarithmic interval.
questions.question: Find the area under the curve \(y=e^x\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=\ln 2\).
questions.explanation:
The area is
\[
\int_{0}^{\ln 2}e^x\,dx.
\]
Since \(e^x\) is its own antiderivative,
\[
\int_{0}^{\ln 2}e^x\,dx
=\left[e^x\right]_{0}^{\ln 2}
=e^{\ln 2}-e^0
=2-1
=1.
\]

questions.learningObjective: Find the area under \(y=\frac{1}{x}\) using the natural logarithm.
questions.question: Find the area under the curve \(y=\frac{1}{x}\) from \(x=1\) to \(x=e^2\).
questions.explanation:
The area is
\[
\int_{1}^{e^2}\frac{1}{x}\,dx.
\]
An antiderivative of \(\frac{1}{x}\) is \(\ln x\) for \(x>0\). Therefore,
\[
\int_{1}^{e^2}\frac{1}{x}\,dx
=\left[\ln x\right]_{1}^{e^2}
=\ln(e^2)-\ln 1
=2-0
=2.
\]

questions.concept: Area Bounded by a Parabola and the x-axis
questions.learningObjective: Determine the area of the region enclosed by a downward parabola and the x-axis.
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by \(y=4-x^2\) and the \(x\)-axis.
questions.explanation:
The curve meets the \(x\)-axis when
\[
4-x^2=0 \implies x=\pm 2.
\]
The area is
\[
\int_{-2}^{2}(4-x^2)\,dx.
\]
An antiderivative is \(4x-\frac{x^3}{3}\). Thus,
\[
\int_{-2}^{2}(4-x^2)\,dx
=\left[4x-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{2}.
\]
At \(x=2\):
\[
8-\frac{8}{3}=\frac{16}{3}.
\]
At \(x=-2\):
\[
-8+\frac{8}{3}=-\frac{16}{3}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{16}{3}-\left(-\frac{16}{3}\right)=\frac{32}{3}.
\]
questions.hint: Find the \(x\)-intercepts first, then integrate the positive curve between them.

questions.learningObjective: Find the area of the region bounded by a parabola and a line.
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=x\).
questions.explanation:
The curves intersect when
\[
x^2=x \implies x(x-1)=0 \implies x=0 \text{ or } x=1.
\]
On \([0,1]\), the line \(y=x\) lies above the parabola \(y=x^2\). Therefore,
\[
\text{Area}=\int_{0}^{1}(x-x^2)\,dx.
\]
Compute:
\[
\int_{0}^{1}(x-x^2)\,dx
=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}
=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}
=\frac{1}{6}.
\]
questions.hint: Find the intersection points, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve.

questions.concept: Area Under a Square Root Curve
questions.learningObjective: Compute the area under \(y=\sqrt{x}\) over a closed interval.
questions.question: Find the area under the curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=4\).
questions.explanation:
The area is
\[
\int_{0}^{4}\sqrt{x}\,dx
=\int_{0}^{4}x^{1/2}\,dx.
\]
An antiderivative is \(\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\). Hence,
\[
\int_{0}^{4}x^{1/2}\,dx
=\left[\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{4}
=\frac{2}{3}\cdot 4^{3/2}
=\frac{2}{3}\cdot 8
=\frac{16}{3}.
\]
questions.hint: Rewrite \(\sqrt{x}\) as \(x^{1/2}\), then use the power rule for antiderivatives.

questions.concept: Area Between a Parabola and a Line
questions.learningObjective: Determine the area enclosed by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\).
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\).
questions.explanation:
The curves intersect when
\[
x^2=2x \implies x(x-2)=0 \implies x=0 \text{ or } x=2.
\]
On \([0,2]\), the line \(y=2x\) lies above the parabola \(y=x^2\). Thus,
\[
\text{Area}=\int_{0}^{2}(2x-x^2)\,dx.
\]
Compute:
\[
\int_{0}^{2}(2x-x^2)\,dx
=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}
=4-\frac{8}{3}
=\frac{4}{3}.
\]
questions.hint: Find the intersection points, then integrate \(2x-x^2\) between them.

questions.concept: Total Area Between Two Symmetric Curves
questions.learningObjective: Find the total area bounded by \(y=x\) and \(y=x^3\) over all intersection intervals.
questions.question: Find the total area of the region bounded by \(y=x\) and \(y=x^3\).
questions.explanation:
The curves intersect when
\[
x=x^3 \implies x(x^2-1)=0 \implies x=-1,0,1.
\]
The total area has two symmetric parts. On \([-1,0]\), \(x^3\ge x\), so the area is
\[
\int_{-1}^{0}(x^3-x)\,dx.
\]
On \([0,1]\), \(x\ge x^3\), so the area is
\[
\int_{0}^{1}(x-x^3)\,dx.
\]
Compute the first part:
\[
\int_{-1}^{0}(x^3-x)\,dx
=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{-1}^{0}
=0-\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}\right)
=\frac{1}{4}.
\]
Compute the second part:
\[
\int_{0}^{1}(x-x^3)\,dx
=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{1}
=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}
=\frac{1}{4}.
\]
Therefore, the total area is
\[
\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
questions.hint: Find all intersection points, split the integral at \(x=0\), and add the areas of the two symmetric regions.
